claim: AAV2-GFP predominantly transduces neurofilament-positive (NF+) neurons in dorsal root ganglia.
source: Of those we examined at 2 weeks post-injection, AAV2-GFP (self-complementary adeno-associated virus serotype 2-enhanced green fluorescent protein) almost exclusively transduced neurons, revealing brightly labeled cell bodies and axons (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing preferential infection of NF+ neurons and quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: A majority of AAV2-GFP transduced neurons were NF+ neurons.
source: Notably, a majority of the transduced, GFP-expressing neurons were NF+ (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1D showing approximately 80% of GFP+ neurons were NF+.

claim: IB4+ neurons rarely express GFP after AAV2-GFP transduction.
source: In contrast, IB4+ neurons rarely were GFP+ and ~30% of GFP+ neurons were CGRP+ (Figure 1D), indicating that NF+ neurons were disproportionately transduced by AAV2-GFP.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 1D showing minimal IB4+ neuron transduction.

claim: AAV2-GFP selectively labels proprioceptive and mechanoreceptive axons within the spinal cord.
source: These findings are the first demonstration that AAV2-GFP predominantly transduces NF+ neurons and selectively reveals their proprio-/mechanoreceptive axons within the spinal cord.
evidence: Supported by data showing GFP+ axons project to deeper layers of dorsal horn and ventral horn where myelinated axons terminate, while superficial laminae lack GFP fluorescence.

claim: Superficial laminae of the dorsal horn (layer I, II) lack GFP fluorescence after AAV2-GFP transduction.
source: In contrast, superficial laminae of the dorsal horn, where small-diameter unmyelinated axons terminate (layer I, II), lacked GFP fluorescence (Figure 1E', E"), showing that AAV-GFP labels few if any IB4+ and CGRP+ axons.
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 1E', E" showing absence of GFP in superficial laminae.

claim: Proprioceptive and mechanoreceptive axons require far more robust long-distance regeneration than nociceptive axons for functional recovery.
source: Therefore, proprio-/mechanoreceptive axons require far more robust long-distance regeneration than nociceptive axons for functional recovery.
evidence: Based on the anatomical fact that NF+ neurons relay signals via second-order neurons in deep spinal cord and distant DC nuclei in medulla, requiring longer regeneration distances.

claim: Myelinated proprioceptive/mechanoreceptive axons regenerate more poorly than nonmyelinated nociceptive axons.
source: Moreover, myelinated proprio-/mechanoreceptive axons regenerate more poorly than nonmyelinated nociceptive axons (Tessler et al., 1988; Guseva and Chelyshev, 2006; Han et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating differential regenerative capacity.

claim: Incomplete lesions occur in approximately 20% of dorsal root crush surgeries.
source: A highly experienced surgeon performed all the root crushes. Nevertheless, incomplete lesions occurred in ~20% of the animals, typically because axons had been spared in the outermost dorsal rootlets (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and quantification from the study's surgical procedures.

claim: After complete root crush in wildtype mice, hundreds of GFP+ axons terminate at similar locations along the dorsolateral spinal cord.
source: After a complete root crush in a wildtype (WT) mouse, hundreds of GFP+ axons all terminated at similar locations along the length of the dorsolateral spinal cord (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by wholemount imaging data showing axon termination patterns.

claim: In wildtype mice, most GFP+ axons terminated within approximately 100 μm of the astrocyte:PNS border.
source: Most axons, however, were located within ~100 μm of the border and only a few axons reached ~200 μm (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 2F showing ~90% GFP+ axons terminated within ~100 μm of the border.

claim: Axons growing farther than 100 μm from the astrocyte:PNS border are considered as having penetrated the DREZ.
source: In the present comparative analyses, we considered axons that grew farther than 100 μm from the border as having penetrated the DREZ (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a methodological definition established for the study's analysis.

claim: Genetic deletion of Nogo, MAG, and OMgp does not enable GFP+ axons to cross the DREZ.
source: Thus, in contrast to the earlier studies that reported robust regeneration of DR axons after pharmacological targeting of myelin signaling, genetic elimination of three major myelin inhibitors did not enable GFP+ axons to cross the DREZ.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Rtn4/Mag/Omg tKO mice showing no enhanced regeneration across the DREZ compared to wildtype.

claim: Inhibiting myelin inhibitors alone is not sufficient to induce regeneration of proprioceptive and mechanoreceptive axons across the DREZ.
source: These results suggest that inhibiting myelin inhibitors alone is not sufficient to induce regeneration of proprio-/mechanoreceptive axons across the DREZ.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing no enhanced regeneration in Rtn4/Mag/Omg tKO mice.

claim: Combined removal of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs enabled only about 10% of axons to cross the DREZ and extend approximately 100 μm beyond it.
source: Those axons that extended across the DREZ were within 200 μm of the astrocyte:PNS border and constituted only ~10% of GFP+ axons (Figure 4F), however, suggesting that additional attenuation of CSPGs in Rtn4/Mag/Omg tKO only modestly promoted regeneration across the DREZ.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 4F showing modest enhancement in ChABC-expressed tKO mice.

claim: Concurrent ablation of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs only slightly enhanced regeneration at 2 weeks post injury.
source: Concurrent ablation of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs only slightly enhanced regeneration, as assessed at 2 wpi, enabling only ~10% GFP+ axons to reach intraspinally ~100 μm past the DREZ.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis comparing ChABC-expressed tKO to wildtype and tKO alone.

claim: Both myelinated and unmyelinated DR axons stop at the DREZ and continue to be immobilized even if myelin inhibitors and CSPGs are simultaneously removed.
source: Collectively, these studies, which represent the first evaluation of DR regeneration in the prolonged and concurrent absence of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs, demonstrate that both myelinated and unmyelinated DR axons stop at the DREZ and continue to be immobilized, even if myelin inhibitors and CSPGs are simultaneously removed.
evidence: Supported by data from 4 week post injury experiments showing no enhanced regeneration in ChABC-expressed tKO mice.

claim: Neither myelin inhibitors nor CSPGs, by themselves or even together, are sufficiently potent to prevent regeneration of most DR axons across the DREZ.
source: Therefore, the minimal regeneration observed in earlier studies targeting CSPGs alone was not due to redundant inhibition by myelin inhibitors. Instead, our findings suggest that neither myelin inhibitors nor CSPGs, by themselves or even together, are sufficiently potent to prevent regeneration of most DR axons across the DREZ.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing minimal regeneration even with concurrent removal of both inhibitor types.

claim: Removal of myelin inhibitors does not enable nerve crush conditioned axons to regenerate beyond the DREZ.
source: Therefore, removal of myelin inhibitors does not enable nerve crush conditioned axons to regenerate beyond the DREZ.
evidence: Supported by data from conditioned Rtn4/Mag/Omg tKO mice showing no enhanced penetration through the DREZ.

claim: A double conditioning lesion modestly enhances regeneration of DR axons across the DREZ in wildtype mice.
source: Quantitative comparisons indicate that the double conditioning lesion enhanced regeneration in WT mice to a level comparable to or slightly greater than a single crush conditioning lesion in Rtn4/Mag/Omg tKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data comparing double conditioned WT mice to other experimental groups.

claim: A double conditioning lesion was far less efficacious than intraspinally expressed GDNF in enabling axons to cross the DREZ.
source: However, it was far less efficacious than intraspinally expressed GDNF, which enabled many more GFP+ axons (>40%) to cross the DREZ and extend deeper in the spinal cord (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I, J; see also Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by comparative quantitative data showing GDNF treatment resulted in >40% axons crossing the DREZ versus ~10% with double conditioning.

claim: Additional removal of CSPGs did not enable significantly more GFP+ axons to penetrate the DREZ in conditioned tKO mice.
source: These results demonstrate that additional removal of CSPGs did not enable significantly more GFP+ axons to penetrate the DREZ in conditioned tKO mice.
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison showing no significant difference between conditioned tKO and ChABC/conditioned tKO mice.

claim: CSPG removal improves penetration of conditioned or unconditioned axons in tKO mutant, but the effect is modest, enabling only approximately 10% axons to extend approximately 100 μm past the DREZ.
source: CSPG removal improves penetration of conditioned or unconditioned axons in tKO mutant, but the effect is modest, enabling only ~10% axons to extend ~100 μm past the DREZ (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by quantitative summary data in Figure 7H.

claim: Myelin inhibitors and CSPGs are not the primary mechanism stopping axons at the DREZ.
source: These findings collectively suggest that the inhibitory role of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs at the DREZ, by themselves or even together, is moderate: they are not the primary factors that arrest even conditioning lesioned DR axons at the DREZ.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing minimal regeneration even with concurrent removal of both inhibitor types and conditioning lesion.

claim: Intraspinal expression of GDNF enabled approximately 50% of GFP+ axons to penetrate the DREZ and extend up to approximately 300 μm from the astrocyte:PNS border in wildtype mice.
source: Quantification indicated that ~50% of GFP+ axons penetrated the DREZ and extended up to ~300 μm from the astrocyte:PNS border (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of GDNF-expressed WT mice in Figure 8D.

claim: Elimination of myelin inhibitors enabled many more GDNF-stimulated axons to extend across the DREZ.
source: Therefore, elimination of myelin inhibitors enabled many more GDNF-stimulated axons to extend across the DREZ.
evidence: Supported by data showing nearly tripling of GFP+ axons at 200 μm from the border in GDNF-expressed tKO compared to GDNF-expressed WT mice.

claim: Elimination of myelin inhibitors enhanced intraspinal regeneration of GDNF-stimulated axons largely by promoting regenerative sprouting or additional branch formation of parental axons at and beyond the DREZ.
source: These findings suggest that elimination of myelin inhibitors enhanced intraspinal regeneration of GDNF-stimulated axons, largely by promoting regenerative sprouting or additional branch formation of parental axons at and beyond the DREZ.
evidence: Inferred from observation that number of axons at 100 μm exceeded number at 0 μm (border), and number at 200 μm exceeded number at 100 μm.

claim: Myelin inhibitors are inhibitory to DR axons and can restrict their regeneration at the DREZ and beyond it within the spinal cord.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that myelin inhibitors are indeed inhibitory to DR axons and can restrict their regeneration at the DREZ and beyond it within the spinal cord.
evidence: Supported by data showing enhanced regeneration of GDNF-stimulated axons in tKO mice compared to wildtype.

claim: Genetic elimination of myelin inhibitors alone or combined with a conditioning lesion promotes minimal regeneration across the DREZ.
source: They also demonstrate that genetic elimination of myelin inhibitors alone or combined with a conditioning lesion promotes minimal regeneration across the DREZ, reflecting their incomplete inhibitory effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tKO and conditioned tKO mice showing minimal enhancement.

claim: Elimination of myelin inhibitors can markedly enhance regeneration only in combination with a treatment that sufficiently enhances intrinsic growth capacity of DR axons.
source: It can markedly enhance regeneration only in combination with a treatment that sufficiently enhances intrinsic growth capacity of DR axons.
evidence: Supported by data showing marked enhancement only when GDNF was combined with myelin inhibitor removal.

claim: Additional removal of CSPGs markedly and synergistically enhanced regeneration of GDNF-stimulated axons across the DREZ in Rtn4/Mag/Omg tKO mice.
source: These findings show that additional removal of CSPGs markedly and synergistically enhanced regeneration of GDNF-stimulated axons across the DREZ in Rtn4/Mag/Omg tKO mice.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing ~20% further increase in axons at 100 μm and ~60% increase at 400 μm in GDNF/ChABC-expressed tKO compared to GDNF-expressed tKO.

claim: CSPGs partially restrict DR axons at and beyond the DREZ.
source: Therefore, like myelin inhibitors, CSPGs partially restrict DR axons at and beyond the DREZ, and their removal can significantly enhance regeneration across the DREZ only when combined with an intervention that sufficiently enhances intrinsic growth capacity of DR axons.
evidence: Supported by data showing enhanced regeneration only when CSPG removal was combined with GDNF treatment in tKO mice.

claim: Co-eliminating myelin inhibitors and CSPGs elicited regeneration of only a few conditioning-lesioned DR axons across the DREZ.
source: Co-eliminating myelin inhibitors and CSPGs elicited regeneration of only a few conditioning-lesioned DR axons across the DREZ.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ChABC/conditioned tKO mice showing minimal enhancement.

claim: The absence of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs markedly and synergistically enhanced regeneration of GDNF-stimulated axons.
source: Their absence, however, markedly and synergistically enhanced regeneration of GDNF-stimulated axons, highlighting the importance of sufficiently elevating intrinsic growth capacity.
evidence: Supported by comparative data showing greatest regeneration in GDNF/ChABC-expressed tKO mice.

claim: There exists a myelin/CSPG-independent mechanism that potently restrains most axons at the DREZ.
source: These findings suggest the existence of a myelin/CSPG-independent mechanism that potently restrains most axons at the DREZ, and that this barrier can be overcome by elevating axon growth capacity, above that achieved by a nerve conditioning lesion.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that even with concurrent removal of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs, most axons fail to cross the DREZ.

claim: Therapeutically targeting both myelin inhibitors and CSPGs can enhance, but will not induce, regeneration of most DR axons into the spinal cord.
source: The results also suggest that therapeutically targeting both myelin inhibitors and CSPGs can enhance, but will not induce, regeneration of most DR axons into the spinal cord.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing enhancement only when combined with growth capacity elevation.

claim: DR injuries commonly result from brachial plexus, lumbosacral plexus, and cauda equina trauma.
source: DR injuries commonly result from brachial plexus, lumbosacral plexus, and cauda equina trauma, and may cause permanent loss of sensation, uncoordinated movement, and chronic pain (Carlstedt, 2008; Kaiser et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: DR axons stop regenerating at the entrance of the spinal cord, the dorsal root entry zone (DREZ).
source: The devastating consequences are because DR axons stop regenerating at the entrance of the spinal cord, the dorsal root entry zone (DREZ), and thus fail to restore connections with secondary neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by multiple studies.

claim: DR axons regenerating along the root quickly stop at the scar-free DREZ, even after a nerve conditioning lesion.
source: Nevertheless, DR axons regenerating along the root quickly stop at the scar-free DREZ, even after a nerve conditioning lesion (Chong et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2007; Di Maio et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating this phenomenon.

claim: A nerve conditioning lesion sufficiently enhances the growth potential of a limited number of dorsal column axons to penetrate a glial scar after spinal cord injury.
source: This potent blockade is surprising because a nerve conditioning lesion sufficiently enhances the growth potential of a limited number of dorsal column (DC) axons to penetrate a glial scar after spinal cord injury (Neumann and Woolf, 1999; Kwon et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myelin-associated inhibitors and CSPGs are conventionally considered responsible for blocking axons at the DREZ.
source: Why the scar-free DREZ is impenetrable even to conditioning lesioned axons remains unclear, but myelin-associated inhibitors and extracellular matrix-associated chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) are conventionally considered responsible (Smith et al., 2012; Mar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles representing the field's conventional view.

claim: Soluble peptides blocking interactions between myelin inhibitors and Nogo receptors dramatically enhance robust functional regeneration of myelinated, but not unmyelinated, axons after DR crush.
source: Soluble peptides blocking interactions between myelin inhibitors and Nogo receptors were observed to dramatically enhance robust functional regeneration of myelinated, but not unmyelinated, axons after DR crush (Harvey et al., 2009; Peng et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Blocking PTPσ, a CSPG receptor, produces functional regeneration of myelinated DR axons into the spinal cord.
source: Similarly, blocking PTPσ, a CSPG receptor, was reported to produce functional regeneration of myelinated DR axons into the spinal cord (Yao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Activating integrins elicits long-distance, topographic and functional regeneration of both myelinated and unmyelinated DR axons.
source: Activating integrins has been found to elicit long-distance, topographic and functional regeneration of both myelinated and unmyelinated DR axons, presumably by counteracting myelin inhibitors, CSPGs and tenascin-C (Tan et al., 2011; Cheah et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two groups found that removing CSPGs alone enables only minimal penetration of DR axons through the DREZ.
source: Although no published studies have contradicted the reports of robust regeneration after pharmacologically targeting myelin inhibitors, two groups have found that removing CSPGs alone enables only minimal penetration of DR axons through the DREZ (Steinmetz et al., 2005; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CSPG removal, when combined with conditioning lesions, neurotrophic factors, or inflammation, has significantly enhanced intraspinal regeneration of DR axons.
source: CSPG removal, however, when combined with conditioning lesions, neurotrophic factors, or inflammation, has significantly enhanced intraspinal regeneration of DR axons (Steinmetz et al., 2005; Wu et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The default assumption has been that myelin inhibitors alone are sufficiently potent to stop axons at the DREZ.
source: Why eliminating CSPGs alone or a nerve conditioning lesion elicits only minimal regeneration across the DREZ is unknown, but the default assumption has been that myelin inhibitors alone are sufficiently potent to stop axons at the DREZ (Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article representing the field's assumption.

claim: This study is the first to genetically target all three major myelin inhibitors simultaneously.
source: Our analysis of triple knockout (tKO) mice lacking Nogo (A, B, C) (also known as Reticulon-4), MAG (myelin-associated glycoprotein), and OMgp/Omg (oligodendrocyte myelin glycoprotein), which is the first to genetically target all three major myelin inhibitors simultaneously, revealed that regeneration across the DREZ is not enhanced.
evidence: This is a novel contribution of the current study.

claim: This is the first combinatorial study to simultaneously eliminate myelin inhibitors and CSPGs.
source: Additionally, we found that supplemental removal of CSPGs in Rtn4/Mag/Omg tKO mice, the first combinatorial study to simultaneously eliminate myelin inhibitors and CSPGs, only modestly enhances regeneration of even conditioning lesioned DR axons.
evidence: This is a novel contribution of the current study.

claim: Targeting myelin inhibitors and CSPGs can markedly enhance intraspinal penetration only when combined with an intervention that elevates axon growth capacity sufficiently robustly, above that achieved by a nerve conditioning lesion.
source: These findings suggest the presence of inhibitory mechanism(s) of remarkably greater potency that potently blocks most axons at the DREZ, and that targeting myelin inhibitors and CSPGs can markedly enhance intraspinal penetration only when combined with an intervention that elevates axon growth capacity sufficiently robustly, above that achieved by a nerve conditioning lesion.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing marked enhancement only with GDNF treatment combined with inhibitor removal.

claim: Proximal axons of large, NF+ neurons are capable of regenerating across the injury site and growing along the root at approximately 1.5 mm/day until they are rapidly immobilized at the DREZ, approximately 4 days post injury.
source: In this crush injury model, proximal axons of large, NF+ neurons are capable of regenerating across the injury site and growing along the root at ~1.5 mm/day until they are rapidly immobilized at the DREZ, ~4 days post injury (Di Maio et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Prolonged elimination of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs for a month after injury did not increase intraspinal penetration.
source: Prolonged elimination for a month after injury also did not increase intraspinal penetration.
evidence: Supported by data from 4 week post injury experiments.

claim: GDNF elicited markedly enhanced intraspinal regeneration in the absence of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs, unlike nerve crush conditioning lesion that produced little enhancement.
source: More surprisingly, GDNF elicited markedly enhanced intraspinal regeneration in the absence of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs, unlike nerve crush conditioning lesion that produced little enhancement.
evidence: Supported by comparative data from GDNF-treated versus conditioned mice.

claim: The limited enhancement with a conditioning lesion was not due to insufficient removal of Nogo/MAG/OMgp or CSPGs.
source: It is unlikely that the limited enhancement with a conditioning lesion was due to insufficient removal of Nogo/MAG/OMgp or CSPGs.
evidence: Supported by the observation that GDNF robustly enhanced regeneration in the same tKO and ChABC-treated mice.

claim: GDNF robustly enhanced regeneration in tKO and produced even more intraspinal regeneration in ChABC-expressed tKO mice.
source: Most notably, GDNF robustly enhanced regeneration in tKO and produced even more intraspinal regeneration in ChABC-expressed tKO mice.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data comparing GDNF-treated groups.

claim: The findings are consistent with earlier observations in WT mice that degrading CSPGs alone or in combination with conditioning lesions elicits minimal intraspinal penetration.
source: Our findings are consistent with earlier observations in WT mice that degrading CSPGs alone (Steinmetz et al., 2005; Wu et al., 2016) or in combination with conditioning lesions (Quaglia et al., 2008) elicits minimal intraspinal penetration.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and consistency with current findings.

claim: The findings demonstrate for the first time that the minimal penetration elicited by the absence of CSPGs was highly unlikely due to synergistic restraint by myelin inhibitors.
source: Importantly, our findings demonstrate for the first time that the minimal penetration elicited by the absence of CSPGs was highly unlikely due to synergistic restraint by myelin inhibitors.
evidence: This is a novel conclusion from the current study's data.

claim: Blocking inhibitors in adulthood may be more effective than eliminating them during development due to compensatory upregulation of other inhibitors.
source: Blocking inhibitors in adulthood may be more effective than eliminating them during development due to compensatory upregulation of other inhibitors (El-Brolosy and Stainier, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study on compensatory mechanisms in genetic knockouts.

claim: CSPGs are the major additional ligands that bind to the Nogo receptor.
source: However, CSPGs are the major additional ligands that bind to the Nogo receptor (Dickendesher et al., 2012), yet co-eliminating CSPGs and myelin inhibitors elicited little penetration through the DREZ.
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: One possible inhibitory mechanism is the expression of additional repellent cues that are upregulated at the axotomized DREZ.
source: One such inhibitory mechanism may be the expression of additional repellent cues that are upregulated at the axotomized DREZ (Andrews et al., 2009; Lindholm et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies identifying upregulated repellent cues.

claim: Most DR axons may be stabilized at the DREZ by forming aberrant synapses rather than dystrophic endings with unknown postsynaptic cells.
source: Another possibility is that most DR axons are stabilized at the DREZ by forming aberrant synapses rather than dystrophic endings with unknown postsynaptic cells (Carlstedt, 1985; Liuzzi and Lasek, 1987; Stensaas et al., 1987; Di Maio et al., 2011; Son, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies suggesting aberrant synapse formation.

claim: DC axons form synapse-like endings on NG2+ cells following spinal cord injury.
source: Consistent with this notion, DC axons form synapse-like endings on NG2+ cells following spinal cord injury (Busch et al., 2010; Filous et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Targeting Nogo, CSPGs, or their receptors in rodent models of spinal cord injury promotes minimal regeneration of myelinated axons, such as corticospinal tract.
source: Targeting Nogo, CSPGs, or their receptors in rodent models of spinal cord injury promotes minimal regeneration of myelinated axons, such as corticospinal tract (Fink et al., 2015; Lang et al., 2015; Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Removal of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs can significantly enhance the growth promotion of a combinatory treatment by stimulating sprouting after spinal cord injury.
source: However, their removal can significantly enhance the growth promotion of a combinatory treatment by stimulating sprouting (Wang et al., 2012; DePaul et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Eliminating myelin inhibitors alone or in combination with CSPG removal markedly enhanced intraspinal regeneration of GDNF-stimulated axons, largely by stimulating regenerative sprouting.
source: Consistent with these observations after spinal cord injury, we found that eliminating myelin inhibitors alone or in combination with CSPG removal markedly enhanced intraspinal regeneration of GDNF-stimulated axons, largely by stimulating regenerative sprouting.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased axon numbers at successive distances from the DREZ.

claim: Removal of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs can allow robust intraspinal regeneration but only when combined with a treatment that sufficiently enhances axon growth capacity.
source: Thus, their removal can allow robust intraspinal regeneration but only when combined with a treatment that sufficiently enhances axon growth capacity.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing robust regeneration only with GDNF treatment.

claim: A single sciatic nerve conditioning lesion does not sufficiently elevate axon growth capacity to overcome the potent myelin/CSPG-independent inhibitory mechanism(s).
source: We found that a conditioning lesion does not sufficiently elevate axon growth capacity to overcome the potent myelin/CSPG-independent inhibitory mechanism(s).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing minimal regeneration in conditioned mice.

claim: A double conditioning lesion only modestly enhances intraspinal regeneration in WT mice, to a level comparable to that found with a single crush lesion in tKO mice.
source: Furthermore, a double conditioning lesion only modestly enhances intraspinal regeneration in WT mice, to a level comparable to that found with a single crush lesion in tKO mice, but that even the double lesion was far less efficacious than GDNF in enabling axons to cross the DREZ.
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison data.

claim: GDNF enhanced penetration of approximately 40% DR axons in WT mice.
source: Although our results highlight the importance of sufficiently elevating axon growth capacity, GDNF enhanced penetration of ~40% DR axons in WT mice.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from GDNF-expressed WT mice.

claim: The intraspinal regeneration elicited by GDNF in the absence of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs was apparently enhanced but did not appear sufficiently robust to power the long-distance regeneration required for proprioceptive/mechanoreceptive axons.
source: Moreover, the intraspinal regeneration it elicited in the absence of myelin inhibitors and CSPGs was apparently enhanced but did not appear sufficiently robust to power the long-distance regeneration required for proprio-/mechanoreceptive axons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that even with maximal treatment, regeneration was limited in extent.

claim: Learning therapeutically applicable treatment of maximizing axon growth capacity must be as important as understanding the myelin/CSPG-independent mechanism that powerfully halts axons at the DREZ.
source: Learning therapeutically applicable treatment of maximizing axon growth capacity must be as important as understanding the myelin/CSPG-independent mechanism that powerfully halts axons at the DREZ, and perhaps also within the damaged spinal cord.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings about the importance of growth capacity elevation.
